html.1: The whole CAE optimization workflow, seen rather than read
html.4: How to find the best design while running as few CAE analyses as possible. Press play below and the whole workflow runs through in order.
html.6: Repeatedly asking "if I analyse this shape, what stress do I get?" is direct analysis. Optimal design runs it backwards — "which shape is lightest while still satisfying the stress limit?" — and lets the computer find it for you.
html.8: From design problem to final check — 7 stages
html.9: Why so involved — can't we just try everything?
html.10: No. With 6 design variables at only 3 levels each, that is 3⁶ = 729 combinations. At one hour per analysis it takes a month. Add one more variable and it triples. So you need a strategy: run a few dozen analyses and cover the rest by prediction. That is stage 2 in the table below.
html.16: Even with the same 20 runs, where you place them changes how much you learn by several times
html.19: Train a model that imitates CAE from those points
html.20: Once trained, a prediction takes 0.001 s — running the optimizer tens of thousands of times is free
html.23: Search for the best combination that meets the targets
html.24: The algorithm finds combinations a person would never reach by hand
html.27: Control the defect rate by accounting for tolerance and scatter
html.28: Drawing values may be exact, but real parts carry error
html.30: Focus of this guide — stages 3 and 4 (optimization and reliability) are the centre of gravity here, but stages 1 and 2 (DOE and surrogates) are covered too, because optimization always runs on top of what they produce.
html.31: Three terms worth pinning down first
html.33: A value you are allowed to change: plate thickness, rib height, a radius. The optimizer moves these around.
html.35: The value you want to minimise or maximise — usually weight, cost or deflection. "Make it light" is an objective.
html.37: A line you must not cross: "stress below 300 MPa", "first natural frequency above 50 Hz". Cross it and the design is out.
html.38: An analogy — think of dieting. The design variables are diet and exercise (things you control), the objective is body weight (to minimise), and the constraint is "keep the muscle" (a line you must hold). Losing the weight by losing all the muscle is a failure, and in the same way a light design that violates a constraint is worth nothing.
html.39: Building design variables — size variables and shape variables (morphing)
html.40: How you create the handles the optimizer turns. Changing one thickness is easy; changing a shape takes a technique.
html.41: Why is this a problem of its own?
html.42: "Plate thickness 2 mm → 2.5 mm" is one number to edit. But what about "round this corner off a bit more"? Change the shape and the mesh has to be rebuilt, which is slow and resists automation. An optimizer needs to repeat this hundreds of times, so it needs a method. That method is morphing.
html.44: Changing shape without rebuilding the mesh
html.47: Variables where only a number changes — plate thickness, beam section area, material properties.
html.48: Substitute one number in the input file and you are done — very simple
html.50: The optimizer can parse the input file and register it as a variable directly
html.52: Variables where the geometry itself changes — corner radius, rib position, surface height.
html.53: Node positions have to move — mesh trouble
html.54: So you build "deformation patterns" in advance with morphing and use those
html.55: Preparation takes effort, but once built it is reused indefinitely
html.56: Why the shape is complex but there are only a handful of variables
html.57:
Open a working file and it feels odd: thousands of nodes, yet only five or six design variables. The reason is that one shape variable moves hundreds of nodes at once.

Treating every node as a variable would give thousands of variables and make optimization impossible. Instead you build "the deformation where this region bulges out like so" once, and hand the optimizer a single number: how much of that deformation to apply. Compressing thousands of degrees of freedom into a few meaningful handles is the heart of morphing.
html.61: The region morphing will move. You mark it to say "deform only the nodes inside this range"
html.62: The grip that pulls that region. Move a handle and the surrounding nodes follow smoothly
html.63: One saved deformation pattern, made by moving handles. This is what becomes a candidate design variable
html.65: The multiplier for how much of a saved Shape to apply. 0 is the original geometry, 1 is the full saved deformation, 0.5 is half. Negative values and values above 1 are usually allowed too
html.66: How it goes in practice — in the pre-processor you set up Domains and Handles and save a few Shapes → the optimization tool picks those Shapes up as design variables automatically → the optimizer only tunes each Shape's multiplier. In other words, the hard part of shape optimization is the preparation, not the optimization.
html.69: Deform too far and elements distort until the analysis diverges. Do not stretch variable ranges beyond reason.
html.71: Apply several Shapes at once and they can overlap into a geometry you did not intend. Check the combined result in advance.
html.73: Inside Tool A you cannot view the deformed mesh directly and have to open a separate viewer — an inconvenience found in hands-on practice.
html.74: How this relates to the rest of the app — the Shape variables built here are, in the end, just a few numbers. So every later stage (DOE → surrogate → optimization → RBDO) proceeds identically whether the variables are size or shape. Shape optimization does not change the algorithm.
html.75: Choosing where to sample — DOE (design of experiments)
html.76: If you only get 20 analyses, where do you put those 20 points? Deciding that is DOE.
html.77: Why not just scatter them anywhere?
html.78: Sample at random and you will inevitably get clusters on one side and empty space on the other. Empty regions carry no information, so the surrogate you build later predicts nonsense there. With the same 20 runs, spreading them evenly buys far more information.
html.80: How each method picks its points — press play
html.82: With three variables — scattering points inside a cube
html.84: Why Box-Behnken needs at least three variables
html.85:
Switch between CCD and Box-Behnken in the 3D demo above. The decisive difference becomes visible.

CCD uses the cube's 8 corners. A corner is the condition where every variable is simultaneously at its maximum (or minimum) — "thickest, widest and tallest all at once". In real experiments such conditions often exceed equipment limits or make the analysis diverge.

Box-Behnken avoids the corners entirely. It uses only edge midpoints — one variable always sits at its middle value while the other two go to their extremes. So the dangerous "everything extreme at once" combination never appears.

But with only two variables the idea of an "edge midpoint" does not exist — in a square, fixing one variable at its centre leaves only the midpoint of a side, which is not enough information to fit a quadratic surface. That is why Box-Behnken is defined only for three variables or more.
html.90:
8 corners + 6 axial + 1 centre
axial points reach α=1.68 beyond the faces
html.91: When extreme conditions are actually runnable. Gives high accuracy for fitting a quadratic surface
html.92:
12 edge midpoints + 1 centre
no corners · one variable always at its middle
html.93: When extreme combinations are risky or impossible. Also cheaper, with fewer points
html.94: Deterministic vs stochastic — what is the difference
html.96: It uses random numbers, so the points land somewhere different every run. Run it twice with the same settings and you get two different results.
html.97: Upside — you can choose the number of points freely
html.98: Downside — an unlucky draw gives a poor layout, so people usually draw several times and keep the best
html.100: Positions follow a mathematical rule, so you get the same points however many times you run it.
html.101: Upside — perfectly reproducible, and anyone else can verify your result exactly
html.102: Downside — you cannot pick the number of points freely (the grid or structure fixes it)
html.103: Check it yourself in the demo above — press the "🔁 Draw again" button under each method and the stochastic ones move while the deterministic ones stay exactly where they were.
html.104: Method summary — what to use when
html.112: The safest default. If the goal is to build a surrogate, this is usually the one. Its strength is staying even when projected onto any single axis
html.115: When you may add more points later. You can keep the points you already have and continue filling in (Sobol)
html.116: Tool A (3)Tool B (Sobol)
html.119: Only when there are very few variables, 2 or 3. Six variables at three levels is 729 runs — not realistic
html.123: When there are many variables and you need to screen first. You give up precision to see quickly which variables matter
html.126:
set by variable count
(2 variables → 9 points)
html.127: When the goal is a quadratic surface model. The aim is not to cover the space evenly but to measure curvature accurately
html.130: When you want a design that is insensitive to environmental noise. Connects directly to RDO (robust design) later
html.131: CCD and Full Factorial have no slider for the number of points — the structure decides it. A two-variable CCD is fixed at 4 corners + 4 axial + 1 centre = 9 points, and with three variables it grows to 8+6+1 = 15. If you want to set the sample count freely, use LHS or Sobol.
html.132: The curse of dimensionality — what the earlier chapters could not show
html.133: Every picture so far used one or two variables. But once the variable count grows, intuition breaks down completely. This is the widest gap between textbooks and practice.
html.134: Read this one carefully — this chapter deliberately breaks the intuition the earlier chapters built. If the two-dimensional pictures left you feeling "twelve points fills the space reasonably well", that feeling is already wrong by the time you have three variables.
html.136: Same number of points, only the dimension grows
html.138: Split each variable into just 3 levels and the number of cells grows like this. The figures below are computed by the app right now.
html.139: To make it concrete — for a 10-variable problem, scanning each variable at only 3 levels gives 59,049 combinations. At one hour per analysis that is 6.7 years, and scattering 100 points touches just 0.17% of the whole. Over the remaining 99.8% of the space, the surrogate is effectively guessing.
html.140: So this is how practice responds
html.141: ① Reduce the variables most important
html.142: Use sensitivity analysis to screen out the variables that do not matter. Cutting 20 variables down to 5 reduces the required number of points astronomically. The earlier chapter presented this as a nice-to-have; in reality it is the step without which you cannot even begin.
html.143: ② Give up on the whole space and look locally
html.144: Abandon the idea of filling the entire space and concentrate only where the optimum is likely to be. ARSM's trust region and EGO's expected improvement are exactly this strategy — the real reason these methods dominate in high dimensions.
html.145: ③ Squeeze out every bit of uniformity
html.146: If you cannot fill it anyway, at least place the points you do have as evenly as possible. The higher the dimension, the wider the gap between pure random and LHS or Sobol — choosing the DOE method matters far more than it did in low dimensions.
html.147: One consolation — fortunately, in real engineering problems not all variables matter equally. Typically 3 to 5 out of 20 drive most of the result (much like the Pareto principle). So once sensitivity analysis has screened them, the effective dimension is lower than you feared and optimization becomes practical. The curse of dimensionality is real, but there is a way around it.
html.149: Past three variables you cannot draw it. So how do you look at the results? This is what production tools actually use.
html.150: How do you fit a six-variable result on one screen?
html.151: Up to 3D you can manage, but from four dimensions there is no way. So you change the premise — instead of standing the axes up in space, stand them side by side and join them with a line. One design becomes one polyline, and even 20 variables fit on a single screen. Tool A's Parallel Coordinate view is exactly this.
html.154: What you read off this picture
html.155: What good designs have in common
html.156: Colour only the top designs and you can see their lines passing through a particular band on a particular axis. You read off a design rule directly: "every good design has variable 2 low."
html.158: Between two neighbouring axes, lines that run parallel mean positive correlation, and lines that cross in an X mean negative correlation. Relationships between variables show at a glance.
html.160: If the good designs are scattered up and down on some axis, that variable has little effect on the result. You can cross-check this by eye against the sensitivity analysis.
html.162: Grey out the designs that break a constraint and the outline of how far the feasible region reaches on each variable appears.
html.163: Relation to the curse of dimensionality — parallel coordinates do not solve the high-dimensional problem. The space is still just as empty. It is a tool for reading as much as possible out of the results you have, and if it shows you "this variable has no influence", you can drop that variable and ease the curse.
html.164: Where to find it in the tools
html.167: Post-Processing → Parallel Coordinate tab. Offered alongside Scatter and the correlation heatmap; a view confirmed in hands-on practice
html.168: The parallel-coordinate view in post-processing — read together with the sensitivity results
html.169: Offered in the results view estimated · not yet confirmed hands-on
html.171: A model that, from a handful of analyses, instantly tells you "with this design the result is roughly here". Once built, predictions are free.
html.173: Optimization has to try designs thousands to tens of thousands of times. Running CAE each time would take years. So you spend 20 analyses building one model, and after that you ask the model instead. An answer arrives in 0.001 s, so tens of thousands of trials are fine.
html.175: Recovering a curve from a few points
html.176: Three representative models — and how differently they behave
html.178: Analogy — approximating mountain terrain with a single large sheet, like a slide.
html.179: Fastest to compute and good for the overall trend
html.180: Does not pass through the points — but is not shaken by noise
html.183: Analogy — throwing several stones into a lake and building the surface from the combined ripples.
html.185: Holds up well even with many variables and strong nonlinearity
html.186: Tries to pass through the noise too — watch for overfitting
html.188: Analogy — a traffic light that passes through the points while also telling you "there is no data near here, I am not confident".
html.189: Passes exactly through the points and reports how untrustworthy each prediction is
html.190: That "not confident" information is what makes EGO and reliability analysis possible
html.191: Why Kriging is special — other models give you only an answer. Kriging gives you the answer plus how much to trust it. The purple band in scene 4 of the demo above is exactly that, and it thickens the further you get from a point. That information is what lets you decide intelligently where to spend the next analysis, which is what makes EGO possible later.
html.192: It would be nice to have just one model — why are there so many?
html.193: Because the winner changes with the character of the data. Below are the errors this app computed just now (smaller is more accurate; scoring is always against the true function).
html.194:
The top two rows and the bottom two are exact opposites.
· Strongly undulating functions (rows 1–2) — a polynomial simply cannot express that shape, so Kriging wins outright.
· A gentle function (row 3) — the shape is expressible by a cubic polynomial, so the error falls to effectively zero (2×10⁻⁹). Here a complex model buys nothing.
· Once noise is added (row 4) — the reason the ranking holds matters. RBF and Kriging try to pass exactly through the points and end up tracing the noise, while the polynomial does not pass through the points and instead smooths across the noise, landing closer to the true function.

The practical call — if the analysis output is clean and the response is complex, reach for Kriging or RBF; if the response is simple, or error is mixed in as with experimental data, look at the polynomial family first.
html.195: Which is why automatic selection exists — Tool A: automatic model selection Tool B: automatic model selection It builds every model and keeps whichever scores best on cross-validation. It takes longer but does not fail, so it is the recommended default in practice.
html.196: Can you trust a surrogate — validation
html.197: A surrogate can pass perfectly through every training point and still be arbitrarily wrong between them. You must check before running the optimizer.
html.198: If we do not know the true function, how do we check?
html.199: That is the key question. Without the answer you cannot mark the paper. The trick is to deliberately hide one of the points you already have — build the model from the rest and see whether it predicts the hidden point. That is cross-validation.
html.201: Scoring by hiding one point at a time — cross-validation
html.203: R² (coefficient of determination) — closer to 1 is better
html.204: "What percentage of the variation in the result does the model explain?" 1.0 is perfect; 0 is no better than always guessing the mean.
html.209: Fair — the trend is right, but re-check near the optimum
html.211: Risky — add points or change the model
html.213: Tells you how far predictions miss on average, in the same units as the result.
html.214: R² is a ratio, so it compares well across problems; RMSE carries units, so it is the one for judging "is this error acceptable in practice?" For example, an RMSE of 3 MPa on a stress prediction is 1% of a 300 MPa allowable — reassuring.
html.215: The most common trap — R² measured on the training points is almost always 1.0. Kriging and RBF are built to pass exactly through those points, so of course it is. That number means nothing. Always look at the cross-validated R² (measured on the hidden point). The demo above shows how far apart the two can be.
html.216: What to do when the score is bad
html.221: Not nearly enough points, or a response too complex for the model to express
html.222: Add more DOE points · try a different model · use automatic selection
html.224: That region has no points. A surrogate only guesses where there is no data
html.225: Concentrate extra points there — ARSM and EGO in the next chapter do this automatically
html.227: Overfitting. Forcing the model through every point makes it oscillate between them
html.228: Try a smoother model (polynomial) · if there is noise, use regression instead of interpolation
html.230: The overall average is fine but the place that actually matters is inaccurate
html.231: Always re-analyse the optimum with real CAE (stage 6 of the whole workflow)
html.232:
Where to find it in the tools — Tool A: the Residuals · Diagnostics tabs of the Fit approach Tool B: cross-validation quality metrics
Tool A shows residuals and cross-validation metrics in a table as soon as you build a surrogate. Do not click past that screen — check it; error you fail to catch here invalidates the entire optimization result.
html.234: How an algorithm handles "lines you must not cross", and when to stop. These are the two things that trip people up most in real runs.
html.235: Can't we just throw away designs that violate a constraint?
html.236: Throwing them away leaves the algorithm with no idea which way to go. If all it hears is "rejected", it cannot tell a small violation from a large one. So most algorithms apply a penalty proportional to the violation, which says not just "bad" but "how bad".
html.239: The optimum almost always sits right on the constraint boundary
html.240:
Why? With a constraint of "stress below 300 MPa", a design sitting at 200 MPa means there is still material left to shave. It could have been lighter and was not. So the optimizer keeps shaving until it stops exactly where the stress equals 300 MPa.

That state is called an active constraint, and when reading an optimization result which constraints are active is the single most useful piece of information — it says "to improve this design further, that constraint has to be relaxed".
html.241: And this is also where RBDO starts — if the optimum sits exactly on the constraint line, then once you allow for scatter half of the parts cross it. The RBDO chapter later deals with this.
html.244: Convergence criteria — the values you set in the tool
html.247: Set it too large / too small
html.248:
Change in the objective
absolute / relative
html.249: Stop when the objective barely moves over the last few iterations. The most basic criterion
html.250:
Too large → stops early, not really converged
Too small → wastes analyses chasing meaningless gains
html.252: Stop when the variables themselves stop moving. Catches the case where the objective is flat but the variables drift
html.253: Sensitive to variable units (mm vs m), so check whether values are normalised
html.255: A safety net. It ends at this count regardless of convergence
html.256: If a run ended here it has not converged — do not take the result at face value
html.258: Treat a very small overshoot (say 0.1%) as satisfied. Needed because of numerical error
html.259:
Too large → answers that really do violate the constraint pass
Zero → it may never converge
html.260: Three things to check whenever you get a result
html.261: Did it converge, or was it cut off at the iteration limit? — the latter is not an answer yet
html.262: Are all constraints satisfied? — one violation makes the design unusable
html.263: Has the convergence curve flattened? — if it oscillates to the end, change the algorithm or the settings
html.264: When it will not work — symptoms and fixes
html.269: Step size too large, or noise in the response makes the gradient come out wrong
html.270: Reduce the step · switch to a surrogate-based method to remove the noise
html.272: The constraints may be impossible to satisfy at all, or the start point is far away
html.273: Remove constraints one at a time to see which one is infeasible · change the start point
html.275: The start point is already a local optimum, or the tolerance is too loose
html.276: Re-run from several different start points · use a global search
html.277: Only one variable goes to its extreme
html.278: A scale difference between variables (thickness 1–3 mm vs length 100–500 mm) makes one of them invisible
html.279: Normalise the variables to 0–1 · reset the ranges realistically
html.281: The surrogate is inaccurate near the optimum
html.282: Check the cross-validation from the previous chapter · add points in that region and retrain
html.283: Optimization algorithms — how the optimum is found
html.284: The problem of finding the lowest point in terrain full of hills and valleys. The methods behave completely differently. This is where the guide focuses.
html.285: Why are there several methods? Can't we just use the best one?
html.286: The fast methods fall into traps, and the ones that do not are slow. That trade-off is the essence of optimization. In the animation below, watch how the two approaches move differently across the same terrain.
html.288: Finding the lowest point on a mountain in fog — two strategies
html.291: Analogy — in fog, feeling only the slope underfoot and walking straight downhill.
html.293: Downside — fall into a small nearby dip and it thinks that is the bottom
html.294: When — the terrain is simple, or you already know a good start point
html.296: Analogy — scattering 20 searchers across the map, radioing each other with "it is lower over here".
html.297: Upside — rarely trapped in a dip. Finds the real minimum
html.298: Downside — 20 searchers means tens of times more analyses
html.299: When — the terrain is complex, or you have no idea where to start
html.300: In practice the answer is often "neither" — if analysis is expensive you cannot afford global search's thousands of runs. So running a global search on top of a surrogate (ARSM and EGO, next page) becomes the workhorse.
html.307: The standard for constrained problems. Approximates with a curved surface and strides downhill
html.309: Moves only in directions that never cross a constraint. Safety first
html.312: Trust-region and quasi-Newton family. Classic methods that numerical libraries expose as individual options
html.315: Crawls like an amoeba by flipping a triangle. Strong on problems with no derivative
html.319: Crossover and mutation between good designs. Almost the only answer for discrete variables like 1.0T / 1.2T thickness
html.323: Like a flock of birds, everyone moves toward the best member. Simpler and faster than GA
html.326: Early on it deliberately moves uphill too to escape dips, then settles down
html.329: Adaptive response-surface family. Detailed next page — the workhorse when analysis is expensive
html.332: Optimization that accounts for scatter. Covered in the RBDO chapter
html.335: When one analysis takes 10 hours, you re-decide "where do I spend the next one?" every single time. The workhorse method in some commercial tools.
html.336: How is this different from what we learned already?
html.337: Until now it was "place all the DOE points → build a surrogate → optimize", done in one pass. But some of those analyses may have been spent nowhere near the optimum. ARSM and EGO start from a few points, look at the result, decide the next point, look again, decide again, over and over. They spend the analysis budget far more carefully.
html.339: Two ways of deciding where to spend one analysis
html.341: ARSM — narrowing in on the promising region
html.343: Analogy — putting a magnifying glass over the area where the treasure probably is and zooming in. If it pays off, go further that way; if not, shrink the region.
html.345: But if it enters the wrong valley at the start, it cannot get out
html.346: GRSM is the version that mixes in global search to reduce that risk
html.347: EGO — deliberately probing where it is unsure
html.349: Analogy — it picks the next point by weighing "probably good" against "unknown because nobody went there".
html.350: Only possible because Kriging supplies an uncertainty band
html.351: It sometimes samples somewhere that looks odd — which is exactly how it finds a hidden valley
html.352: It wastes a few analyses early in exchange for rarely getting stuck in a local optimum
html.353: A comparison point — whether a tool has this family or not makes the biggest difference on expensive real problems. It matters far more than "how many algorithms are listed", so highlight this row in any comparison table.
html.354: Finding the variables that matter — sensitivity analysis
html.355: Even with 20 design variables, usually only 3 or 4 actually move the result. Screening them first makes everything afterwards much cheaper.
html.357: Optimizing all 20 variables needs hundreds of analyses; keep only the important 4 and a few dozen will do. The other 16 do not change the result anyway, so you can fix them at reasonable values.
html.359: Shake the variables and the culprit reveals itself
html.360: The variable that is quiet alone but loud in company
html.361: An analogy — in cooking, salt changes the taste dramatically on its own (large main effect). Lemon juice, though, does little by itself but transforms the dish when added with sugar. Testing lemon juice "on its own" and dropping it as "no effect" would be a serious mistake.
html.362: So sensitivity is always read as two numbers.
html.363: Main effect — influence on its own
html.364: How much the result changes when only that variable moves.
html.365: Total effect — influence including its company
html.366: Total contribution including interactions with other variables. If this is large, never drop the variable.
html.367: Where people go wrong — look at variable 3 in the chart above. Its main effect is nearly zero but its total effect is substantial. Judging by the main effect alone and deciding "no influence, drop it" throws the entire optimization result off.
html.374: Nudges variables one at a time and watches the response. Quickly narrows down "who the culprit is"
html.377: Takes the total variation in the result as 100% and splits it into each variable's share. Captures interactions exactly
html.380: Decomposes contributions using a surrogate predictive-power metric or game theory (SHAP)
html.383: Keeping it from breaking — RBDO (reliability-based design)
html.384: The drawing says 10.0 mm but real parts come out 9.9–10.1 mm. Designing with that scatter in mind is RBDO. This is where the guide focuses.
html.385: Isn't the optimization we have learned so far enough?
html.386: No, and the reason is startling. The optimization so far produces a design that "just satisfies" the constraint, and once you allow for scatter that design has a defect rate of exactly 50%. Below is why.
html.388: Why designing "just to the line" makes half the parts defective
html.389: MPP — the central idea in reliability analysis
html.390:
The problem — to get the defect rate exactly you would have to build a million parts and count the failures (Monte Carlo). With hours per analysis, a million runs is impossible.

The fix — among all the ways it can fail, find the single most likely one. That location is the MPP (Most Probable Point), and measuring the distance to it gives you the defect rate directly. A million runs collapses into a few dozen.
html.391: How it appears in the tools — the same capability is exposed differently. Some tools hand you the MPP vector directly; others expose it only under SORA-family algorithm names. Which approach a tool takes is the comparison point.
html.392: Buying safety means paying in performance
html.400: The result of deterministic optimization — unusable
html.409: β (beta) is the number that says "how many standard deviations lie between the mean and the failure line". Larger β is safer, but it also means a thicker, heavier, more expensive design. Setting that trade-off is what RBDO does.
html.410: Reducing scatter buys safety for free — every margin in the table above is a multiple of σ (the scatter). So if you improve the process and halve σ, the same safety level costs half the margin. Tightening quality control is as valid a strategy as thickening the design — and that is where the next chapter, RDO, begins.
html.416: Every step the optimizer takes, an inner loop finds the MPP all over again. Accurate but slow (the classical approach)
html.419: Today's mainstream. Finish an ordinary optimization first, pull the constraint wall inward by the safety margin, then optimize again. Much faster
html.422: When there are several failure modes, considers them together from a whole-system view
html.424: Simply run tens of thousands to millions of random trials and count. Impossible with real analysis; realistic only on top of a surrogate
html.426: If RBDO is "do not break", RDO is "come out the same every time". Designing to reduce scatter rather than the mean.
html.427: If nothing fails, why care about scatter?
html.428: Performance that varies from part to part becomes a quality problem. If one car pulls well and the next feels flat, the complaints arrive. And a sharp optimum is only good on the drawing — in real production, a small deviation makes performance collapse.
html.430: A deeper valley vs a wider valley — where do you place the design?
html.431: RBDO and RDO — the distinction on one page
html.433: The question — "is the probability of breaking below target?"
html.434: Concern: the tail of the distribution (how far it reaches into the failure region)
html.435: Method: push the design toward the safe side
html.436: Result: heavier, but it does not break
html.438: The question — "how much does performance differ between parts?"
html.439: Concern: the width of the distribution (how spread out it is)
html.440: Method: move the design point to a location insensitive to scatter
html.441: Result: slightly worse mean performance, but consistent
html.443: By crossing an array of factors you can control with noise factors you cannot, it finds the combination whose performance holds steady as the environment changes. This is where DOE's orthogonal arrays are used.
html.446: It changes the objective from "mean performance" to "mean + weight × scatter" — exactly the pink curve in the demo above. Raise the weight and stability counts for more.
html.447: When there are two goals — multi-objective optimization
html.448: "Light and strong" pull in opposite directions. Here the answer is not one design but a set of compromises.
html.449: Can't we just add the two objectives into one?
html.450: You can, but you have to fix the weights in advance — "weight matters 7, stiffness 3". And how do you choose those weights? Worse, as shown below, some answers can never appear no matter how you set them.
html.452: The frontier of compromises — the Pareto front
html.453: A modified genetic algorithm. It ranks individuals by who is not beaten by whom, and within a rank it favours individuals that are far apart, so the answers spread evenly across the whole frontier.
html.454: The decisive difference from a weighted sum — a weighted sum gives you one answer per set of weights. NSGA-II gives you the entire frontier in a single run. So you can see the whole picture of what trade-offs exist before deciding.
html.456: Support for every method covered above — compiled while studying three commercial tools hands-on.
html.457:
⚠ Always read the evidence level alongside
confirmed seen directly in the GUI during practice · documented from official documentation · estimated unconfirmed
Many Tool B and C entries were compiled from documentation, so they are marked "documented/estimated". The distinction is kept so that confirmed and estimated are never mixed.
html.486: 3. Optimization algorithms Tool A confirmed hands-on
html.509: Three things that matter when building a comparison table
html.510: The "number" of local-optimizer options creates an illusion in tool comparisons — classic methods like Trust-region, L-BFGS-B, CG, TNC, Powell and Nelder-Mead are easy to fill in from a numerical library.
html.511: What matters is that adaptive response-surface (ARSM/GRSM) and SORA-family methods are supported by few tools, and those are far more important on real, expensive CAE problems. Their presence decides more than the count does.
html.512: Some tools do not expose the RBDO algorithm name at all. Until you have confirmed which approach it uses (double loop / SORA / single loop), marking it "unconfirmed" is the honest entry.
html.523: Every chart here is not a picture but a result the browser computed live (LHS and Sobol sequences, Kriging, PSO, Pareto dominance and the rest are implemented directly). Open the 🔬 self-verification panel at the foot of each page to see the values the app computed at run time checked against the mathematical answer.

Limits — these are models reduced to one or two design variables to make them understandable. On real problems (dozens of variables, many constraints) the ranking between methods can change, and in particular the way space empties out as variables are added is not something a two-dimensional picture can convey.

js.47: This is the whole map of design optimization. It flows from top left to bottom right. Press play and each stage explains what it does, one at a time.
js.48: 1. Define the problem — decide what you can change (design variables), what you want to improve (the objective), and what must be respected (constraints). Get this wrong and everything after it is meaningless.
js.49: 2. Choose sample points (DOE) — you only get a few analyses, so plan where to probe in advance. The key is spreading points evenly through the design space.
js.50: 3. CAE analysis — actually run an analysis at each chosen point. This is over 90% of the total cost. At hours per run, reducing the count is everything.
js.51: 4. Train the surrogate — build a smooth surface through the points you obtained. Now you can predict "with this design, roughly this value" instantly, without running an analysis.
js.52: 5. Search for the optimum — like a ball rolling downhill on the surrogate, find the best point. Predictions are free, so tens of thousands of trials are fine. This is the focus of the guide.
js.53: 6. Verify the optimum — take the optimum the surrogate proposed and run it through real CAE once more. If prediction and reality disagree, improve the surrogate and go back.
js.54: 7. Account for uncertainty — the drawing says 10.0 mm but reality is 9.9–10.1 mm. Allow for that scatter and shift the design so defects do not occur. Also a focus of the guide.
js.55: That is one full lap. In practice you often loop back from 6 to 4, and ARSM and EGO, covered later, are the methods that automate that loop.
js.64: The stage where the design problem is written not as equations but as 'change what, to improve what'
js.65: Spread points evenly through the design space — analyses are run only at these points
js.68: The most expensive stage — which is why cutting the number of runs is the heart of optimization
js.69: Join the points into a model that predicts without running an analysis
js.70: Find the optimum on the surrogate, like a ball rolling downhill
js.74: Always confirm the prediction matches reality — if not, go back and fix the surrogate first
js.77: Think of a spread distribution, not a single drawing value — the tail is the defect rate

js.85: This is the structure's mesh. The analysis computes on this grid of elements. Optimization wants to keep changing the shape.
js.86: Size variables are easy. "Plate thickness 2 → 2.5" edits one number in the input file, and the mesh is untouched.
js.87: Shape is the problem. Modify the CAD to change the geometry and the mesh has to be rebuilt from scratch — slow, and it fails often when automated. And the optimizer needs to do this hundreds of times.
js.88: The morphing idea — do not rebuild the mesh; pull the existing nodes instead. The red dot is a handle, and the nodes around it follow smoothly. Element connectivity is unchanged, so the analysis still runs.
js.89: Saving one such deformation gives you a Shape. The optimizer receives a single number: how much of this deformation to apply — 0 for the original, 1 for the full saved amount, 0.5 for half.
js.90: This is the key point — there are hundreds of nodes but only one design variable. One number moves hundreds of nodes at once. That is why a complex working file has so few variables.
js.91: You can also build several Shapes and combine them. Add a second deformation (the blue handle) and there are two variables, with the optimizer tuning both multipliers together.
js.92: Careful — deform too far and elements distort until the analysis diverges (shown in red). So the range of a shape variable must stay within what the mesh can take.

js.106: Measure the error at the training points and it is all zero. R² comes out at 1.000. But that number means nothing. The model was built to pass through those points, so of course it does.
js.107: What you actually want to know is what happens between the points. The grey dashed line is the truth, and as you can see some stretches are badly off. In a real situation you never get to see that grey line.
js.108: So you use cross-validation. The method is simple — deliberately hide one point and rebuild the model from the remaining seven.
js.109: Then see whether it predicts the hidden point. The red line is the gap between prediction and reality — a real error you can measure without knowing the answer.
js.110: Repeat this once for every point. With 8 points you build the model 8 times.
js.111: Here is the result. Training R² was 1.000 but cross-validated R² is far lower. This is the trustworthy report card.
js.112: In short — ignore the training score and look only at the cross-validated one. If it is bad you need more points or a different model; run the optimizer anyway and you get the wrong answer.

js.143: This is the design space. Darker is a better (lighter) design, and it improves toward the top right. With no constraints you would simply go to the top-right corner.

js.146: The algorithm does not simply discard violating designs. It adds a penalty proportional to the violation — a little for a small breach, a lot for a large one. Only then can it tell which way to head back.
js.147: Here is the terrain with the penalty added. Outside the boundary it has become a steep hill. Now the algorithm is naturally pushed back inside.
js.148: Look at the optimum (the star). It sits exactly on the constraint line. Improving further would mean crossing it, which is not allowed, so the point right against the line is the answer.
js.149: This is the outcome of almost every optimization — the optimum sits on the constraint boundary (an active constraint). js.164: The question is "when do we stop?" Keep going and it keeps improving by a tiny amount — the issue is whether that tiny amount is worth a few more hours of analysis.

js.166: Set the tolerance large and it finishes early. You save analyses but receive an under-converged answer. A common mistake in practice.

js.547: Deterministic optimization compares only the means. It decides "mean strength = mean load, so it fits exactly and needs no more thickness" and stops here. It is the lightest, after all.
js.548: Now plot margin = strength − load. If this value is below 0, the part breaks.
js.549: A startling result — exactly half of the distribution lies left of 0. A 50% defect rate. One in every two parts you build breaks. That is what designing on means alone gives you.

js.611: We built 400 designs and evaluated two objectives at once. The horizontal axis is weight, the vertical is deflection — lower is better on both. So the further toward the bottom left, the better the design.
js.612: Many of them need not be considered at all. Some designs are heavier and deflect more than another design — losing on both objectives means elimination (grey).
js.613: What survives is the pink frontier — the Pareto front. None of these designs beats another, because improving one objective necessarily worsens the other.
js.614: So which one do you pick? A common approach is a weighted sum — setting a ratio like "weight to deflection = 5 to 5". The black line is that ratio, and the point where it first touches the frontier (orange) is chosen.
js.615: Change the weights and the choice moves with them. Favour weight and it goes left, favour deflection and it goes right — sweeping along the frontier.
js.616: But when the frontier curves inward like this, there is a problem. Turn the weights anywhere from 0 to 100 and the middle section is never chosen. The line always touches one of the ends first.
js.617: The conclusion — a weighted sum simply cannot reach some compromises. So in practice you use a true multi-objective algorithm such as NSGA-II to obtain the whole frontier first, then look at the picture and choose.

meta.title: Optimal Design Visual Guide — DOE, Surrogates, Optimization, Reliability
meta.desc: A visual, animated guide to the whole CAE optimal-design workflow. Every chart is computed live in the browser, and each chapter carries its own self-verification.
